analysis.one_liner: Repeals the Affordable Care Act and replaces it with tax credits, high-risk pools, and looser insurance rules.
analysis.headline: The full repeal-and-replace bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced, never got a hearing or vote, and finished with zero cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have repealed the Affordable Care Act in its entirety, effective as if it had never passed, and rebuilt health coverage policy from scratch. In its place it offered a refundable tax credit for low-income people buying their own insurance, a deduction for other individuals, association health plans and membership associations that could bypass state insurance rules, interstate insurance sales, medical malpractice limits, and an antitrust exemption letting doctors negotiate jointly with insurers. It explicitly declined to require insurers to sell coverage to everyone at community rates, and it barred the children's insurance program from covering children in families above three times the poverty line.
analysis.who_benefits: Uninsured and self-employed people buying their own insurance would get a refundable credit worth up to $2,000 a month for an individual plus $500 per dependent (capped at two dependents), phasing down as income rises above 200% of poverty; higher-income buyers would get a deduction instead. Health insurers would gain freedom from community rating and guaranteed-issue mandates, from state benefit mandates through association plans and interstate sales, while still receiving the tax credits as premium payments. Physicians would gain a malpractice shield, an antitrust exemption for joint negotiation with insurers, freedom to privately contract with Medicare patients, and preemption of state limits on what they can charge. Small employers would get a credit for auto-enrolling workers and a choice architecture letting employees take employer money to any insurer.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Insurers, doctors, small employers, the self-insured

how_it_helps.text: Creates a refundable, advanceable tax credit for health insurance costs for low-income individuals, worth up to $2,000 per month for an individual ($4,000 on a joint return) plus $500 per dependent, phasing down one percentage point for each $1,000 of income above 200% of the federal poverty guideline, and paid directly to insurers on the taxpayer's behalf.

Allows an above-the-line tax deduction for the cost of qualified health insurance for taxpayers above the credit's income range, capped at the average value of the employer-sponsored insurance tax exclusion.

Establishes individual and small employer membership associations (IMAs) under the Public Health Service Act and association health plans under ERISA, letting individuals and small employers band together to buy coverage, and preempts state benefit-mandate laws for coverage sold through an IMA.

Appropriates $300 million a year for fiscal 2014-2016 for state high-risk pools and reinsurance mechanisms to cover people priced out of the underwritten individual market, with funding sunsetting after October 1, 2016.

Gives physicians an exemption from federal and state antitrust laws when negotiating contract terms with health plans, lets Medicare beneficiaries privately contract with doctors, preempts state limits on professional charges, and lets doctors claim a bad-debt deduction for uncompensated emergency care.

Changes malpractice litigation: compliance with HHS best-practice guidelines changes the burden of proof, states get grants to create administrative health tribunals, and claimants can receive future damages as periodic payments.

Lets group plans vary premiums and cost-sharing by up to 50% based on participation in a wellness program, and gives small employers a credit of up to $1,500 for establishing auto-enrollment and defined-contribution health benefits.

analysis.who_pays: People with pre-existing conditions would bear the biggest cost: the bill states that nothing in it mandates guaranteed issue or community rating, so insurers could once again deny or surcharge coverage based on health status, with high-risk pools and a $300 million-a-year grant program as the fallback. Families above 300% of the poverty line would lose CHIP eligibility for their children. The Medicaid expansion and the ACA's premium subsidies would disappear. State consumer protections — required benefits, limits on provider charges, malpractice rules — would be preempted for much of the individual market, and patients suing over medical errors would face a higher burden of proof and administrative tribunals. The bill also prohibits federal funds or the new credits from paying for any health plan covering abortion beyond life-endangering cases, rape, or incest.
analysis.who_pays_short: People with pre-existing conditions, states, malpractice plaintiffs

drawbacks.text: Section 3 states that nothing in the bill shall be construed to provide a mandate for guaranteed issue or community rating in the private insurance market, so insurers could deny or price coverage based on health status; protection for sick people would rest on voluntary insurer rules and a modestly funded, time-limited high-risk pool program.

The bill repeals the ACA and the health provisions of the Health Care and Education Reconciliation Act effective as of their 2010 enactment, erasing the Medicaid expansion, the ACA's premium tax credits, and the individual market's guaranteed-issue and community-rating rules.

It prohibits CHIP payments for children with family income above 300% of the poverty line and requires state CHIP plans to specify how they will reach 90% of targeted low-income children, narrowing the children's coverage program.

It preempts state laws governing benefits offered through IMAs and prohibits states from limiting the charges health professionals can bill, removing state-level cost and consumer protections from much of the individual market.
The new tax credit counts at most two dependents and is capped at fixed dollar amounts, so larger low-income families would receive no additional credit for a third child or more.

It allows premiums and cost-sharing to vary by up to 50% based on wellness-program participation and requires CHIP outreach before expanding eligibility, shifting more cost and responsibility onto individuals.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill made a genuine offer to people shut out of the pre-ACA individual market: a substantial refundable credit paid straight to insurers, a tax deduction for everyone else, and pooling mechanisms for small employers and individuals. But it paid for consumer choice by dismantling the rules that protected the people who need coverage most. Removing guaranteed issue and community rating — the ACA's core protections — would leave people with cancer, diabetes, or any pre-existing condition dependent on high-risk pools funded at $300 million a year nationwide, an amount far below what universal guaranteed-issue coverage costs, and the funding would sunset after 2016. Combined with the CHIP income cap, the preemption of state benefit mandates and charge limits, and malpractice changes that make it harder to win, the design traded security for flexibility in a way that fell hardest on the sick, children in modest-income families, and states. A fair assessment is that the credits helped some uninsured people while the repeal exposed millions of covered people to losing protections they already had.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced in the Senate on December 18, 2013 and referred to the Finance Committee the same day; the committee never took it up, no vote ever happened, and the Congress ended on January 3, 2015 with the bill still sitting in committee.

narrative.text: Senator John McCain introduced the Empowering Patients First Act of 2013 in the Senate on December 18, 2013.

The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance on the day of introduction, and the action history shows no further action — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — before the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015.
No senator from either party cosponsored the bill; the cosponsor list is empty.

The bill would have repealed the ACA and the health care provisions of the 2010 reconciliation act retroactively to their enactment and restored prior law, replacing them with tax credits, association plans, interstate insurance sales, malpractice reforms, and an antitrust exemption for physicians.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died without a vote, the ACA's guaranteed-issue, community-rating, Medicaid expansion, and premium subsidy protections remained in place; the people covered by them were better off, while insurers, doctors, and self-employed buyers did not get the deregulation and tax benefits the bill offered.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: People relying on ACA coverage protections

for.name: John McCain
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in the Senate on December 18, 2013 and delivered introductory remarks; no senator joined him as a cosponsor.

against.name: Max Baucus (until Feb 2014) and Ron Wyden
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never scheduled it for a hearing or markup; the committee record shows no action after referral.

against.name: Harry Reid
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor; no floor vote on the bill ever occurred in the 113th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: A Republican senator introduced the bill alone with zero cosponsors from either party, and the Democratic-controlled Senate Finance Committee and Democratic Senate leadership took no action on it.

industries.note: The bill would have freed insurers from guaranteed-issue and community-rating mandates, let them sell across state lines and through IMAs and association plans that preempt state benefit mandates, while still making them the paid channel for the new tax credits. Their gain came directly from the ability to underwrite and surcharge the sick, which is the cost ordinary people with pre-existing conditions would have borne.

Doctors would have gained an antitrust exemption for negotiating with health plans, a malpractice shield built on best-practice guidelines and administrative tribunals, preemption of state limits on their charges, Medicare private contracting, and a bad-debt deduction. Some of this (joint bargaining with insurers) could benefit patients, while the malpractice limits and charge preemption would reduce patient recoveries and state price oversight.

A credit of up to $1,500 for adopting auto-enrollment and defined-contribution plans, plus rules letting employees redirect the employer contribution to any insurer, would have cut small employers' health benefit costs and paperwork.
